newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal pilots prepare legal fight over strike.
newsitem.headline: Portugal pilots prepare legal fight over strike.

text.p: Pilots at TAP-Air Portugal were preparing to take their battle over working hours to court as the struggling airline cancelled three more flights on Monday.
Planes bound for Amsterdam, Zurich and Munich were grounded despite a government decree on Saturday ordering the pilots' union to call off a selective strike.
A spokesman for the loss-making company said stranded passengers were being switched to other airlines. He did not expect any further cancellations on Monday.
"We have had to cancel three flights but we do not expect any more problems today," Raul Alves Fernandes told Reuters.
The Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres approved a decree on Saturday forcing members of the Civil Aviation Pilots' Union (SPAC) to return to normal working.
Pilots had been refusing to fly any route subject to a late scheduling change, something which airlines are frequently forced to do during the busy summer tourist season.
As with seven cancellations over the weekend, the trouble on Monday was due to pilots calling in sick or having already worked more than the statutory 45 hours in the past week, Fernandes said.

The airline said that there were 15 pilots currently off work ill compared with three at the same time last year. Fernandes said that it was not yet clear whether any of the pilots involved were defying the government order, which carries the risk of a jail sentence.
The government had invoked special powers granted under the constitution, where the public interest is deemed at stake.
But leaders of the pilots' union, which says that TAP is trying to make them fly more hours than is safe, say that they will challenge the government ruling in the courts.
Union vice-president Angelo Felgueiras told journalists on Monday that the government move actually violated the constitution because it amounted to an effective ban on the right to strike.

He said the decree could in any case not be used against the pilots because they were not refusing to provide a normal service. The partial stoppage had only been aimed at last-minute changes to scheduling.

The government hopes to privatise partly the airline before the end of the decade and secure a strategic partnersphip with one of the world's leading carriers. Both steps are seen as vital to TAP's survival in an increasing competitive world.
But sector analysts say any such moves will be impossible until TAP, which had been hoping to make a small profit in 1997, sorts out its labour problems.

The company says its pilots, particularly those flying long-distance routes, put in fewer hours than competing airlines. Pilots say the problem lies in the inefficiency of the airline and that more pilots are needed.
